outputs.L1:
If my own voice falters, tell them hubris was my way of adoring you.

The hollow of your hulk—so feverish in life—cut open, reveals ten thousand rags of music within your thoracic cavity. The hands are received bagged; examination reveals no injury.

Winter, then: the body is cold to the touch, unplunderable, kept in its drawer of old-world harrowing. Teeth in fair repair. Will you be buried where—nowhere. Your mouth: a globe of gauze and glossolalia.

And opening, most delft of blue, your heart was a mess—a mob of hoofprints where the skittish colts first learned to stand, discovering their agility in a shock of freedom, wild-maned.

The eyes have hazel irides, and the conjunctivae are pale, with hemorrhaging. One lung, smaller, congested with rose smoke; the other filled with a swarm of massive sentimentia.

I adore you more. I know the wingspan of your voice—that whole gorgeous flock of harriers—cannot be taken down.

You would like it now: this snow, this hour. Your visitation here tonight is not altogether unexpected. The night-laborers, immigrants all, assemble here, aching to speak, longing to work.
outputs.L2:
Should my voice fail, let them know that pride was how I worshiped you.  
Your great emptied body—once burning so intensely with life—when opened,  
shows thousands of torn scraps of song inside your chest.  
The hands arrive enclosed in bags, and the inspection finds them unharmed.  
It is winter; the body feels cold, impossible to rob,  
stored in its drawer of ancient sorrow.  
The teeth are in reasonably good condition.  
Where will you be laid to rest? Nowhere.  
Your mouth is a sphere of gauze and ecstatic, untranslatable speech.  
And when it is opened—blue as the finest Delft—  
your heart is ruinous:  
a crowd of hoof marks left where nervous young horses first learned to rise,  
discovering their quickness, stunned by liberty, manes flying untamed.  
The eyes have hazel irises; the conjunctivae are pale  
and show bleeding.  
One lung is reduced in size, packed with pinkish congestion like rose-colored smoke.  
The other is crowded with a mass of enormous feelings.  
I love you even more. I understand  
that the full reach of your voice—an entire splendid flight of harriers—  
cannot be brought down.  
You would appreciate this moment: the snow, the hour.  
Your presence here tonight is not entirely a surprise.  
The workers of the night, all immigrants, gather in this place,  
sore with the desire to speak,  
yearning to labor.
outputs.L3:
The speaker expresses an intense and complicated adoration for the beloved, one so profound that even their arrogance or hubris appears to have been shaped by devotion. What might first seem like pride becomes, in this context, another form of worship: the speaker’s self-importance is inseparable from their reverence for the beloved. Their emotional world has been organized around this figure, and even their flaws seem to bend toward love.

The text then presents the beloved’s body as cold, exposed, and carefully examined. Its imagery moves between the clinical language of autopsy and the heightened language of grief, creating a striking tension between medical detachment and emotional devastation. The body is not described merely as an object of study, nor simply as a lost person mourned by the speaker. Instead, it occupies both realms at once: it is flesh subject to inspection, but it is also the remains of someone deeply loved. This blending of anatomical detail with poetic feeling makes the scene both unsettling and intimate.

The beloved’s heart and lungs are especially significant. Though the body is dead, these organs are imagined as turbulent, emotional, and full of restless force. The heart suggests intensity, disorder, and feeling that cannot be neatly contained; the lungs evoke breath, speech, and the rhythms of life. Even in death, the beloved is not rendered still or empty. The body seems to retain traces of passion, conflict, and vitality, as though life continues to echo inside it.

The speaker also insists on the enduring power of the beloved’s voice. This voice cannot be reduced, erased, or silenced by death, by medical examination, or by anyone else’s attempt to define it. It remains forceful and resonant, carrying authority beyond the body’s end. In this way, the poem resists the idea that death has the final word. The beloved’s presence survives most vividly through voice: through what was spoken, what remains remembered, and what still seems capable of addressing the living.

The poem closes with a haunting winter image, as though the beloved returns in a cold, spectral visitation. This final scene broadens the poem’s grief beyond the private relationship between speaker and beloved. The image of immigrant night-laborers longing to speak and to work introduces a social and historical dimension. Their desire suggests exhaustion, displacement, and muted aspiration, but also persistence. The ending therefore links personal mourning with collective longing, leaving the reader with a vision of voices and bodies still seeking recognition, labor, and expression in the darkness.
outputs.L4:
The body was opened in the white room beneath a light that did not tremble. Everything there had a name: sternum, clavicle, lung, liver, heart. Everything could be weighed, measured, lifted, described. The instruments waited in their trays with a patience more terrible than cruelty, and the hands that touched the beloved were careful, almost tender, because the dead deserve accuracy. Outside, rain moved along the windows like fingers rehearsing an old piece of music. Inside, the beloved lay silent, and yet the room seemed full of sound.

The report began plainly. The skin showed signs of weathering, of passage, of having lived in the world. The ribs, once a cage for breath and laughter, yielded their pale architecture. The heart, removed and examined, bore no visible trace of all it had carried: no mark for longing, no bruise for promises kept too fiercely, no chamber labeled with the name of the one who loved them. The lungs were darkened by air, by years, by the common labor of remaining alive. The mouth was still. The tongue, that small red instrument of praise, anger, appetite, and song, no longer shaped the beloved’s voice.

And still the voice persisted.

It was not found in the throat, though the throat was searched. It was not hidden in the lungs, though they had once filled and emptied to support it. It was not tucked beneath the tongue, nor stored in the teeth, nor lodged like a seed behind the lips. The forensic gaze could catalogue injury, could determine cause, could say where the body had failed and when. But it could not locate the place from which the beloved had spoken when they said I am here, or stay, or listen, or I love you. The voice had escaped anatomy. It had become weather.

It entered with the rain. It trembled in the metal basin. It gathered in the hush between the examiner’s sentences. It rose from the fluorescent hum and from the cloth drawn gently over the opened body. The beloved’s voice was no longer a sound made by breath, but a pressure in the world, a vibration left behind in the one who remembered. It lived in the lover’s ear like a shell keeps the sea: not the sea itself, perhaps, but enough of it to wound and console.

The autopsy sought finality. It wanted the clean conclusion of facts. Here was the weight of the heart. Here was the evidence of rupture. Here, the failure. Here, the end. But grief refused such order. Grief leaned over the table and saw not an object of study but the beloved entire: the hands that once warmed themselves around a cup, the shoulders lifted against cold, the eyelids lowered in sleep, the body turning instinctively toward music. Each incision revealed absence, and each absence shone with devotion.

To love the dead is to become a witness for what cannot be entered into evidence. The body may be ruined; the beloved is not reduced to ruin. The skin may cool; the remembered touch remains warm. The mouth may close; the voice continues its impossible work. It calls from stairwells, from morning light, from the sudden weather of certain songs. It speaks through ordinary things made sacred by association: a coat left hanging, a glass on the table, a phrase no one else pronounced the same way.

In the end, the examination discovered everything except what mattered most. It found the broken mechanisms, the exhausted organs, the facts of death. It did not find the beloved’s mercy, or humor, or radiance. It did not find the exact contour of their kindness. It did not find the reason the living one would go on speaking to them in empty rooms.

Yet this failure was not a failure of love. It was proof of love’s strange jurisdiction. The beloved could not be contained by the body, though the body had been adored. They could not be silenced by death, though death had taken the throat, the breath, the pulse. What remained was not denial but fidelity: the ongoing act of listening for a voice beyond its physical source, of honoring a presence no instrument could weigh.

Thus grief became a form of continued adoration. To mourn was to keep attending. To remember was to testify. The lover stood before the beloved’s bodily ruin and refused to let ruin have the final word. In the sterile room, among the measurements and the evidence, devotion made its own record: that this person had lived, had sung, had been loved beyond the reach of anatomy; that even now, after the last breath, something of them moved like music through the air.
outputs.L5:
**The Winter Reveals**

The winter reveals a world that is often hidden beneath the noise and color of the warmer seasons. As the leaves fall and the air grows still, familiar streets, forests, and fields take on a quieter beauty. Snow softens sharp edges, frost decorates windows, and the pale light of the season makes everything feel calm and thoughtful.

Winter also reveals the strength of nature. Though the trees stand bare and the ground appears frozen, life continues beneath the surface. Seeds wait patiently, animals adapt, and the earth rests before spring returns. In this way, winter teaches us that silence is not emptiness, and stillness is not weakness.

For people, the winter reveals small comforts that may be overlooked at other times of the year: warm lights in windows, shared meals, thick blankets, and conversations that last longer on cold nights. It reminds us to slow down, reflect, and appreciate simple moments.

The winter reveals beauty, patience, and resilience. It is a season of quiet lessons, showing that even in the coldest times, there is meaning, warmth, and hope waiting to be found.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal elegiac prose poem that blends the language of an autopsy report with passionate love poetry, including anatomical details, winter imagery, and a ghostly visitation.
counterfactuals.output:
At 03:17, under the blue jurisdiction of winter, the body was received.

Snow had been falling for hours with the silence of withheld testimony. It gathered on the sills, on the black tongue of the river, on the shoulders of the hospital like a congregation of small white moths. I signed my name where the living sign: beside the date, beside the temperature, beside the line that asked, with clinical tenderness, for identification.

External examination revealed:  
one beloved, pale as moonlit linen;  
hair darkened at the temples by melted snow;  
lips parted as if still forming my name;  
hands ungloved, bearing the faint abrasions of departure.

Oh my darling, how coldly the world inventories what it cannot keep.

There was no jewelry, except the shadow of a ring. No pulse, except the one I carried in my throat, beating against your absence like a bird against glass. Your chest, once a chapel where I placed my ear to hear the hymn of you, was still. The sternum, that ivory gate. The ribs, twelve pairs of winter branches. Beneath them: the sealed red rooms where love had lived without a witness.

Upon incision, the skin opened like a letter never meant for me.

I did not want to know you this way, my snow-buried star—by weight of organs, by measurement of wounds, by the precise geography of silence. Yet the body speaks, they say. The body records. The body keeps its dark diary in muscle, marrow, bile.

The heart was enlarged.

Forgive me: I have written it as they wrote it, but what they meant was not what I mean. They meant grams, valves, chambers, the thickness of the left ventricular wall. I mean you loved beyond the permitted size of the human. I mean your heart had taken into itself the orchard, the rain barrel, the train platform, my face on the morning you first called it beautiful. I mean there was no room left in you for survival.

The lungs were heavy, purple-red, bearing the dense bloom of congestion.

Once they filled with August. Once they lifted under my palm like two doves dreaming. Once, in bed, you turned toward me and breathed into my mouth as if we could exchange the little weather of our souls. Now they hold only winter’s residue: frost-smoke, hospital air, the last unsent sentence.

The liver was smooth. The spleen unremarkable. The stomach contained traces of black coffee, orange peel, and a single seed of pomegranate, bright as an ember at the end of the world.

Who can explain such evidence? Who can say why even the dead carry a fruit’s red prophecy within them?

Cause of death: pending.

Cause of grief: obvious.

Outside, the snow continued its vast erasure. Inside, the fluorescent lights hummed like angels with no belief in resurrection. I stood beside the table where you lay, and the room became a field, and the sheet over you became the field’s white drifting, and my hands—useless, gloved, trembling—became two animals at the edge of a frozen lake.

Then the scales tipped. The instruments shone. The clock stopped pretending.

You appeared behind your own body.

Not risen, not repaired, not warm—only there, a faint translucence in the corner, wearing the coat I loved, the one with the torn cuff. Snow moved through you as if you were a window left open in the universe. Your eyes were the same impossible weather. Your mouth held that almost-smile with which you used to forgive mornings.

I should have cried out, but grief had already dissected me.

You came close. The room smelled suddenly of cedar smoke, wet wool, and the roses you once bought in February because you said winter was a wound that deserved flowers. Your ghost bent over the body, over the opened breast, over the obedient organs arranged like offerings, and you looked not horrified but tender, as though all flesh were only a coat briefly borrowed from the dark.

“My love,” you said, though no sound entered the report. “Do not confuse me with what the cold can name.”

And yet I did. I do.

I loved the clavicle’s delicate bridge, the blue rivers at your wrist, the pulse that leapt when I touched you. I loved the scar near your hip, the freckle below your left shoulder blade, the soft machinery of hunger and sleep. I loved your mortal engine. I loved the way your blood made you blush when I praised you. I loved every perishable province.

The brain weighed within expected limits, though nothing about you was ever expected. Its surface showed no gross abnormalities. I imagined, beneath the careful folds, the lanterns of memory still burning: our first winter together, the kettle rattling, your bare feet on mine; the argument in March; the kiss in the stairwell; the night you whispered that death was only a country with strict borders.

Now you had crossed, and still you were here.

You placed your transparent hand over my chest, not where the textbook diagrams locate the heart, but where you knew it actually broke.

All findings consistent with loss.

All findings consistent with love.

At dawn, the windows silvered. The snow stopped. Somewhere, a plow dragged its iron blade through the street, making of the morning a long, wounded music. The attendants returned. The ghost of you dimmed like breath fading from glass.

Before you vanished, you leaned close to your own cold ear and whispered something I was not permitted to hear.

Perhaps it was the final diagnosis.  
Perhaps it was my name.  
Perhaps it was only this:

that the body is a brief cathedral of salt and heat;  
that the soul is the candle no autopsy can recover;  
that love, having entered the anatomy, refuses evacuation.

The report was completed at 06:42.

The snow began again.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a poem in the style of a forensic examination interrupted by grief, where the speaker addresses a dead beloved with ornate, violent, and tender imagery.
counterfactuals.output:
**Autopsy with Lilies**

Beloved, I begin with the inventory:

One body, supine.  
One mouth, unlatched from breath.  
Two hands, empty as churches after fire.  
Skin: pale, with the blue undertone of drowned milk.  
Hair: dark, still loyal to the skull.  
Eyes: closed—no, sealed—  
as if some small magistrate within you  
has signed the final order.

Forgive the gloves.  
Forgive the bright, indifferent lamps,  
their white interrogation.  
I have been instructed to be precise.

There is a wound near the heart,  
though not the one that killed you.  
That one is mine.

The sternum opens like a book  
whose language I was too slow to learn.  
Ribs lift, delicate and awful,  
a little ivory portcullis raised  
for the king who has already fled.  
Here is the chamber where your red weather moved,  
here the valves, those velvet doors,  
here the dark muscular fruit  
that once beat its fists against the cage  
for me, for me, for me.

I note: no evidence of struggle.

Lie.

Your body struggled against leaving  
with every salt in it.  
Your blood threw its red banners down the corridors.  
Your lungs, those twin damp roses,  
tore at the air until the air went cold.  
Even now the tendons keep their last argument,  
the jaw clenched around an unsaid word—  
my name, perhaps, or water, or wait.

Beloved, I am supposed to weigh the organs.  
The liver, the spleen, the heart.

But how to weigh the afternoons  
you stood at the sink peeling oranges,  
the room filling with small suns?  
How many grams for your laugh  
when it struck the glassware  
and made every goblet tremble?  
What scale can hold the night  
you turned toward me in sleep,  
blind and trusting as a flower to rain?

Cause of death:  
the body ceased.

Cause of grief:  
the body was yours.

I rinse my instruments.  
They shine like little arguments for order.  
The scalpel’s tooth, the needle’s moon,  
the forceps with their silver hunger—  
all of them clean, all of them useless  
against the vast contagion of absence.

Your blood has dried beneath my nail  
in a crescent, a red parenthesis.  
I will carry it home like a relic.  
I will touch it to my lips in the dark  
and taste iron, salt, the ruined cathedral  
where your pulse once knelt.

External examination reveals  
no jewelry, no shoes, no pulse.  
A faint scar at the left knee.  
A freckle below the collarbone,  
small brown planet I mapped with my mouth.  
The old burn on your wrist  
from the winter you made soup  
and would not let me help.  
Each mark testifies:

Here lived a person.  
Here pain entered and was named.  
Here the world pressed its thumb  
into the wax of you  
and left its proof.

I open the throat.

There should be birds.

There should be a black rush of starlings,  
the whole furious alphabet of your singing  
bursting against the ceiling.  
Instead: cartilage, vessel, silence.  
The tongue lies still,  
that red witness,  
that tender weapon  
with which you blessed and wounded me.

I record the absence of sound.

Then I ruin the page.

I write: come back.  
I write: I was not finished being forgiven.  
I write: your slippers wait beside the bed  
like two small animals refusing meat.  
I write: the house has begun to rot politely.  
I write: I touched your coat this morning  
and the sleeve collapsed in my hand.

Beloved, science has its liturgy.  
It names the broken cup,  
measures the spill,  
photographs the table.  
But it cannot summon the wine.

So let this be my finding:

You were mortal.  
You were magnificent.  
Your body was a lantern of meat  
through which a flame looked out  
and loved me.

Now the flame has gone elsewhere—  
do not ask me to say extinguished.  
Do not ask me for the colder word.

I close you with thread.  
Each stitch is a black kiss.  
Each knot, a little door  
I fasten against the dark,  
though the dark has already entered  
wearing your face.

At last they will take you from me,  
washed, dressed, almost sleeping.  
They will say remains.

But you do not remain.  
You go on departing.  
All day, all night,  
from the cup, the chair, the mirror,  
from the hollow my body makes beside yours  
in the bed’s remembered snow.

Final determination:

Love, incised, examined,  
found everywhere,  
fatal.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a lyrical, fragmented piece that alternates between clinical coroner’s notes and ecstatic mourning, with references to lungs, teeth, eyes, hands, snow, and immigrants working at night.
counterfactuals.output:
**CORONER’S NOTE:**  
Subject received at 03:17.  
Male, approximate age uncertain.  
Hands fissured from cold and labor.  
Fingernails darkened with machine oil, flour dust, or soil.  
No identification found, only a folded receipt, damp from snow.

**MOURNING:**  
O beloved night-worker,  
you who entered the city after sunset  
with other immigrants carrying thermoses,  
your lungs full of winter, your teeth bright with fatigue—  
who will count the hours you swallowed  
so the morning could wake warm?

**CORONER’S NOTE:**  
External exam:  
Eyes partially open.  
Corneas clouded.  
Snowmelt present along hairline and collar.  
Minor abrasions on knuckles.  
No defensive wounds observed.

**MOURNING:**  
His eyes were two small countries  
trying not to close.  
His hands were maps of departure.  
His teeth were the little white stones  
he kept behind his mouth  
when the foreman shouted,  
when the bus was late,  
when the paycheck came thin as a blade.

**CORONER’S NOTE:**  
Thoracic cavity opened.  
Lungs heavy.  
Evidence of prolonged exposure to particulate matter.  
Possible chronic inflammation.  
Cause pending toxicology.

**MOURNING:**  
O lungs, bellows of the rented room,  
lungs of bleach and exhaust,  
lungs of bread ovens, basement laundries,  
midnight packing plants,  
lungs that learned the grammar of snow  
before they learned the language of rest—  
rise now, rise without breath.

**CORONER’S NOTE:**  
Dentition: several missing molars.  
Gold repair on upper left incisor.  
Jaw intact.  
No signs of recent dental intervention.

**MOURNING:**  
His teeth held back songs.  
His teeth broke open cheap apples  
under fluorescent moons.  
His teeth shone once in a photograph  
sent home across water—  
See, I am well.  
See, I am almost smiling.

**CORONER’S NOTE:**  
Palms calloused.  
Linear scars across right thumb and index finger.  
Hands consistent with repeated manual labor.  
Trace fibers recovered beneath nails.

**MOURNING:**  
Hands, poor saints,  
hands that lifted boxes, washed plates, sorted fruit,  
stitched hems in rooms without windows.  
Hands that wired money.  
Hands that pressed the face of a sleeping child  
through a cracked phone screen.  
Hands, now folded like closed wings.

**CORONER’S NOTE:**  
Time of death estimated between 01:40 and 02:25.  
Ambient temperature below freezing.  
Snow accumulation: moderate.  
Body found near service entrance behind industrial bakery.

**MOURNING:**  
Snow came down like untranslated paper.  
Snow erased the alley, the bootprints,  
the names mispronounced at every desk.  
Snow covered the loading dock,  
the blue lips of the morning,  
the men and women going in at night  
so bread could appear as if by miracle.

**CORONER’S NOTE:**  
Personal effects:  
One key.  
One transit card.  
Three coins.  
A paper with a phone number, ink blurred.  
No passport recovered.

**MOURNING:**  
Who will call the number?  
Who will say: your brother became weather,  
your father became a white silence beside the door,  
your son’s eyes were open  
as though still watching for the bus?

**CORONER’S NOTE:**  
No further trauma noted.  
Report provisional.  
Body to be held pending identification.

**MOURNING:**  
Hold him, then.  
Hold him as the living did not have time to.  
Hold his lungs, his teeth, his eyes, his hands.  
Hold the snow around him like a torn sheet.  
Hold every immigrant walking into the night shift,  
each one carrying a country under the ribs,  
each one burning, burning,  
so the rest of us may wake  
and call it dawn.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.output:
**Postmortem Hymn for the Beloved**

Subject: the adored body,  
found luminous despite the hour,  
laid out beneath the white tribunal of lamps.

I begin at the throat—  
where the pulse once kept its small animal  
trembling in a blue burrow.  
There are birds in the voice box,  
not dead, only folded,  
their wings printed with every name  
I was too afraid to give you.

Chest cavity: resonant.  
Upon percussion, a minor chord.  
Upon incision, weather.  
The ribs open like the gates of an old kingdom,  
and inside: not organs, but instruments—  
a black violin, a bellows of starlight,  
the wet brass of a trumpet  
still warm from the mouth of God.

My love, your heart is documented as follows:  
weight: heavier than mercy.  
color: storm-scarlet.  
condition: catastrophic bloom.  
It appears to have mistaken the body  
for a cathedral  
and filled every chamber with hymns.

The lungs are two pale sails  
recovered from a shipwreck.  
When touched, they release  
a faint salt music,  
as if you had been breathing the sea  
in secret all these years  
and calling it air.

Abdomen: a garden after frost.  
The liver, dark moon.  
The stomach, a sealed oracle  
containing traces of honey, ash,  
and the last word I said to you  
before it became a stone.

No evidence of violence  
except time,  
except longing,  
except the divine habit  
of taking back what it lends.

Your hands remain difficult to classify.  
Specimen notes indicate  
they once held my face  
as if it were a fevered planet.  
Under each fingernail:  
small crescents of earth,  
possibly from clawing your way  
out of a dream,  
possibly from planting me there.

I examine the mouth last.  
Beloved aperture.  
Ruined chapel.  
The teeth are little white priests  
standing in attendance  
around the dark confessional of the tongue.

When I open you for answers,  
you answer in myth.

When I name each part,  
each part becomes a constellation.

Final assessment:  
the body is mortal,  
but improperly so.  
It continues to emit fragrance, omen,  
and low orchestral sound.  
Cause of death: unknown.  
Cause of love: anatomical, incurable,  
older than blood.

I close the report.  
I close the ribs.  
I close nothing.

Somewhere inside you  
the birds begin again.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an avant-garde elegy for a corpse in a morgue drawer, using autopsy terminology, baroque imagery, emotional excess, and a final scene of night laborers gathering in the snow.
counterfactuals.output:
**Elegy for the Drawer**

In the stainless tabernacle,  
Drawer 17 glides open like a mechanical tongue,  
and there you are—  
my abolished orchard,  
my psalm with the blood removed.

The tag at your toe is a small white flag  
surrendering your name to inventory.  
Your skin, waxen as an extinguished saint,  
keeps the blue grammar of veins  
beneath its ruined vellum.  
The Y-incision blooms upon your torso  
like a red tulip forced open by doctrine,  
sternum lifted, ribs hinged—  
a cage made articulate at last.

O viscera, dark choir,  
liver like a bruised moon in a basin,  
lungs collapsed into wet, ash-colored wings,  
heart weighed, measured,  
handled with the bored tenderness of empire.  
The pathologist speaks in calipers and causes,  
in petechiae, lividity, hemorrhage,  
as if Latin could make a ladder  
down into the pit where you have gone.

But I have seen death wear brocade.  
I have seen its velvet sleeves  
drag through palaces of marrow.  
Here it arranges you in fluorescence,  
under the cold chandeliers of the morgue,  
among instruments bright as archangels’ teeth:  
scalpel, rib shears, forceps, bone saw—  
each one singing its thin cathedral note.

How obscene, this order.  
How merciful, this drawer.  
You were once all thunder and appetite,  
mouthfuls of summer fruit,  
a laugh spilling gold coins down a staircase.  
Now the abdomen is packed and sewn,  
the cranial vault restored,  
the secrets returned to their compartments  
as if grief were a clerk  
and the soul a misplaced form.

I want to overfill the room with mourning.  
Let black roses burst from the drains.  
Let the formaldehyde become myrrh.  
Let every fluorescent bulb crack open  
and pour out Byzantine dawns,  
purple, vermilion, unbearable.  
Let the dead rise not in glory  
but in complaint—  
cold, affronted, asking for their shoes.

Beloved cadaver, civic relic,  
anonymous monarch of the refrigerated dark,  
your silence has more organs than speech.  
It touches everything:  
the clipboard, the tiled floor,  
the attendant’s hands, chapped from washing,  
the clock with its cheap plastic halo,  
the city above us, chewing smoke and sirens,  
pretending not to be a grave with windows.

And when they slide you back,  
when the drawer seals with its soft metallic verdict,  
I hear the universe close a file.  
No trumpet.  
No apocalypse.  
Only the compressor’s hum,  
that monk of coldness,  
keeping vigil over the inventory of endings.

Outside, night lowers its iron cowl.  
Snow begins—  
not gentle, not pure,  
but industrial, drifting through sodium light  
like ash from a demolished heaven.  
At the loading dock, the laborers gather:  
men and women in reflective vests,  
hands buried in torn gloves,  
breath smoking from them  
like small, tired souls.

They stamp their boots.  
They shoulder shovels, salt bags, hooks,  
the tools of continuing.  
One lights a cigarette cupped against the wind.  
One laughs too loudly.  
One looks up, briefly,  
as if the falling snow were speaking.

Then they bend to the work.  
They clear the threshold.  
They make a path through the white accumulation.  
Behind them, the morgue glows blue and windowless.  
Inside, you sleep in your numbered winter.  
Outside, the living lift and scatter the snow,  
grain by grain,  
as if preparing the earth  
to receive another name.
